title: Geometry
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L geometry curriculum: coordinate and analytic geometry of conics, geometric transformations (isometries, similarities, affine maps), vectors in geometry, and an introduction to non-Euclidean geometry.

questions.question: The standard equation of a circle with centre (a,b) and radius r is:
questions.explanation: This is the locus of points at fixed distance r from the centre (a,b), derived directly from the distance formula.

questions.question: The standard form of an ellipse centred at the origin with semi-major axis a and semi-minor axis b is:
questions.explanation: This is the standard Cartesian equation of an ellipse, reducing to a circle when a = b.

questions.question: The eccentricity e of an ellipse satisfies:
questions.explanation: An ellipse has eccentricity strictly between 0 (a circle) and 1 (the parabolic limit), distinguishing it from parabolas (e=1) and hyperbolas (e>1).

questions.question: The standard form of a hyperbola centred at the origin, opening along the x-axis, is:
questions.explanation: The minus sign between the squared terms is the defining algebraic feature that distinguishes a hyperbola from an ellipse.

questions.question: The asymptotes of the hyperbola x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1 are given by:
questions.explanation: As x and y grow large, the hyperbola approaches the lines obtained by setting the equation's right-hand side to zero, giving y = ±(b/a)x.

questions.question: The standard form of a parabola with vertex at the origin opening rightward is:
questions.explanation: This equation describes all points equidistant from the focus (a,0) and the directrix x = -a, the defining property of a parabola.

questions.question: A parabola is defined as the locus of points equidistant from:
options: A fixed point (focus) and a fixed line (directrix)
questions.correct_answer: A fixed point (focus) and a fixed line (directrix)
questions.explanation: This focus-directrix property is the fundamental defining characteristic of a parabola, and of conics generally in terms of eccentricity.

questions.question: An ellipse is defined as the locus of points where:
options: The sum of distances to two fixed foci is constant
The difference of distances to two fixed foci is constant
The distance to a single focus is constant
The product of distances to two foci is constant
questions.correct_answer: The sum of distances to two fixed foci is constant
questions.explanation: This sum-of-distances property (equal to 2a, the major axis length) is the classical definition of an ellipse.

questions.question: A hyperbola is defined as the locus of points where:
options: The absolute difference of distances to two fixed foci is constant
The sum of distances to two fixed foci is constant
All points are equidistant from one fixed point
The distance to the origin is constant
questions.correct_answer: The absolute difference of distances to two fixed foci is constant
questions.explanation: This difference-of-distances property distinguishes the hyperbola from the ellipse's sum-of-distances property.

questions.question: A translation in the plane that maps point (x,y) to (x+h, y+k) is an example of:
options: An isometry (rigid transformation) that preserves distance and shape
A transformation that changes the size of a figure
questions.correct_answer: An isometry (rigid transformation) that preserves distance and shape
questions.explanation: Translations preserve all distances between points and hence preserve shape and orientation, making them rigid motions.

questions.question: Under a rotation about the origin by angle θ, the point (x,y) maps to:
options: (x cosθ − y sinθ, x sinθ + y cosθ)
(x cosθ + y sinθ, x sinθ − y cosθ)
questions.correct_answer: (x cosθ − y sinθ, x sinθ + y cosθ)
questions.explanation: This is the standard 2D rotation matrix applied to the point, derived from combining the components along the rotated axes.

questions.question: Reflecting the point (x,y) across the x-axis gives:
questions.explanation: Reflection across the x-axis keeps the x-coordinate fixed and negates the y-coordinate.

questions.question: A dilation (scaling) transformation with scale factor k about the origin maps (x,y) to:
questions.explanation: A dilation uniformly scales the coordinates by the factor k, enlarging (k>1) or shrinking (0<k<1) the figure while preserving shape.

questions.question: Which of the following is preserved under a similarity transformation but not necessarily under a general affine transformation?
options: Ratios of lengths along a line
questions.explanation: Similarity transformations (isometries composed with uniform scaling) preserve angles, while general affine maps preserve parallelism and ratios along lines but can distort angles.

questions.question: An affine transformation of the plane can be written in the form:
options: T(x) = Ax + b, where A is an invertible matrix and b a translation vector
T(x) = Ax only, with A orthogonal
questions.correct_answer: T(x) = Ax + b, where A is an invertible matrix and b a translation vector
questions.explanation: General affine maps combine a linear transformation (matrix A) with a translation (vector b), generalizing isometries and dilations.

questions.question: The composition of two rotations about the same point, by angles θ1 and θ2, results in:
options: A single rotation by angle θ1 + θ2 about that point
questions.correct_answer: A single rotation by angle θ1 + θ2 about that point
questions.explanation: Rotations about a common centre compose by simply adding their angles.

questions.question: Two triangles are said to be congruent if:
options: One can be mapped onto the other by an isometry (preserving both shape and size)
They have the same shape but possibly different sizes
questions.correct_answer: One can be mapped onto the other by an isometry (preserving both shape and size)
questions.explanation: Congruence requires an exact match under a rigid motion, unlike similarity which only requires equal shape.

questions.question: Two figures are similar if:
options: One can be mapped to the other by a similarity transformation (isometry combined with uniform scaling)
They lie on the same line
questions.correct_answer: One can be mapped to the other by a similarity transformation (isometry combined with uniform scaling)
questions.explanation: Similar figures have the same shape (equal corresponding angles, proportional sides) but not necessarily the same size.

questions.question: Given position vectors a and b of two points A and B, the vector representing the displacement from A to B is:
questions.explanation: The vector from A to B is found by subtracting the initial point's position vector from the terminal point's.

questions.question: The midpoint M of the segment joining points with position vectors a and b is given by:
questions.explanation: The midpoint's position vector is the average of the two endpoint position vectors.

questions.question: Vectors u and v are perpendicular if and only if:
questions.explanation: The dot product of two vectors equals |u||v|cosθ, which is zero exactly when θ = 90 degrees.

questions.question: The locus of points equidistant from two fixed points A and B is:
options: The perpendicular bisector of segment AB
A line through A and B
questions.correct_answer: The perpendicular bisector of segment AB
questions.explanation: Every point equidistant from A and B lies on the line that is perpendicular to AB and passes through its midpoint.

questions.question: In spherical (non-Euclidean) geometry, the sum of the interior angles of a triangle is:
questions.explanation: On a sphere, positive curvature causes triangle angle sums to exceed the Euclidean value of 180 degrees, growing with the triangle's area.

questions.question: In hyperbolic geometry, the sum of the interior angles of a triangle is:
questions.explanation: Hyperbolic geometry has negative curvature, which causes triangle angle sums to fall short of the Euclidean 180 degrees.

questions.question: Euclid's parallel postulate, whose modification distinguishes non-Euclidean from Euclidean geometry, states that:
options: Through a point not on a given line, exactly one line can be drawn parallel to the given line
Parallel lines are always the same length
Every triangle has exactly one right angle
questions.correct_answer: Through a point not on a given line, exactly one line can be drawn parallel to the given line
questions.explanation: Non-Euclidean geometries arise by replacing this postulate: hyperbolic geometry allows infinitely many such parallels, spherical geometry allows none.

questions.question: The set of all isometries of the plane that map a given regular polygon onto itself forms:
options: A symmetry group (dihedral group) of the polygon
questions.correct_answer: A symmetry group (dihedral group) of the polygon
questions.explanation: The collection of rotations and reflections preserving a regular n-gon forms the dihedral group of order 2n under composition.

questions.question: In projective geometry, two distinct lines in the projective plane:
options: Always meet at exactly one point (including points at infinity)
questions.correct_answer: Always meet at exactly one point (including points at infinity)
questions.explanation: Projective geometry extends the Euclidean plane with points at infinity so that even parallel Euclidean lines meet there, eliminating the exception of non-intersecting lines.

questions.question: A shear transformation of the plane, e.g. (x,y) -> (x + ky, y), preserves:
questions.explanation: A shear has determinant 1 (area-preserving) but is not an isometry, so it generally distorts angles between lines.

questions.question: The distance between two points (x1,y1) and (x2,y2) in the Cartesian plane is given by:
questions.explanation: This is the Euclidean distance formula, derived from the Pythagorean theorem applied to the coordinate differences.

questions.question: A general second-degree equation Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0 represents an ellipse when the discriminant B^2 - 4AC is:
questions.explanation: The sign of the discriminant B^2 - 4AC classifies the conic: negative for an ellipse, zero for a parabola, positive for a hyperbola.

questions.question: For the general second-degree conic equation, a positive discriminant B^2 - 4AC indicates the conic is:
questions.explanation: A positive discriminant value in the general conic equation signals hyperbolic type.
